prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which made structural empirical industrial organisation a credible basis for analysing market power, mergers and regulation

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. I moved from B027 (Kiyotaki and Moore) in round 1 to B005 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn). The chair asked for one test applied to all four leading candidates. I would use these questions. Did the work change what can be credibly known? Has that been validated in use or in evidence, and not only in theory? Is the credit attributable to a small, coherent set of people? Is the work mature enough that its lasting influence is observed, not predicted? Under that test B005 does best on the combination. Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes solved a specific problem, estimating demand for differentiated products with endogenous prices and unobserved quality, and made substitution patterns, markups and merger effects measurable. The record of use includes merger review, regulation, trade, health and environmental analysis. The credit is a jointly authored core, and the work is about three decades old. B027 remains the candidate I find conceptually most original. Its attribution is as clean as B005's. It fares worse on the validation limb, because direct identification of the amplification mechanism is indirect and it sits next to the 2022 prize. In round 1 I put conceptual originality above breadth of use. On reflection, I applied that weighting to my own field, where I am most prone to read familiarity as merit. B005 is also no weaker on originality. It created a new way of measuring, and a measurement advance that changes what can be learned is a discovery. I would keep the citation narrow, on demand and competition in differentiated-product markets. Pakes's dynamic-industry work is a real strength, but the three-name credit rests on the BLP core.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a methods prize without a single headline substantive finding. A committee that weights an explanatory result about how the economy works above a measurement advance could rank B005 below B027 or B014. The three-name cap excludes Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, who have real claims to the wider empirical-IO tradition. BLP-type estimates are also sensitive to instruments, functional form and implementation. That is a limit on how much applied results can be treated as settled, even if it does not undercut the originality of the method. I weight the replication and use record because that is the evidence I can see in the openings. I have not verified it independently, and members from IO have a stake in that field. By contrast, I have no specialist authority to settle the Bresnahan-versus-Levinsohn question beyond the attribution logic of the citation.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B005 first. He argues that BLP is cleanly attributable and validated in practice, and that the test is whether work changed what can be credibly learned about welfare and policy questions. He also cites my own round-1 concession that direct identification of the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is more contested than its theory.
responses.response: I agree with the test and now apply it to B027 as strictly as to B005. B027 is conceptually foundational and cleanly credited. B005 has more direct validation, because regulators and applied researchers have exercised it in many settings. That difference is why I moved. I also accept his reading of the overlap concern. My round-1 argument that the 2022 prize concerned bank runs and intermediation while Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral-constrained borrowers still holds as a distinction. But it is something the Committee must argue, and I have not verified how it would be received.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B027 first and lists B005 as his first alternative. He was moved by the breadth-of-use argument but would apply it equally to Kiyotaki-Moore and would not rank a toolkit above a mechanism merely because the toolkit has more documented applications.
responses.response: His objection to ranking by application count is fair, and I do not rely on a count. My reason for moving is that B005 meets the same test with a stronger validation record, not that more fields use it. Our shared co-authorship means my moving should not be read as independent confirmation of either of us, and I take the same caution about his staying. I still agree with him on B027 attribution and on leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist. If the Committee instead gives conceptual originality decisive weight, B027 is my first alternative, and the choice between us is a weighting difference, not a factual dispute.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B014 first and says he would move to B005 if the overlap with the 2024 institutions prize were judged decisive. He also holds that the B014 trio is cleanly attributable and the work mature, and he credits B014's empirical programme as more extensively tested than B027's.
responses.response: I take the claim that B014 is better tested than B027 seriously. It is also why B014 stays among my alternatives. My remaining hesitation is the one he states: cross-country identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is weaker than the repeated use that has tested the BLP estimators. I agree that the distinction between policy choice under given rules and long-run origins of institutions is real. I have not verified how far the Committee would accept it. I would not call the overlap objection decisive. I would not rank B014 above B005 on the common test while the identification question stays open. If Fredriksson's Persson-Tabellini two-person fallback were adopted, that would narrow the exposure without removing it.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first and revised his third name from Bresnahan to Levinsohn, because a demand-estimation citation should credit all three authors of the paper it rests on. He discloses that his own IO background may bias him toward B005.
responses.response: I agree with the revision and with the attribution logic. I considered Bresnahan and would use him only under a deliberately broader empirical-IO citation, with the credit set and wording changed together. I also take his bias disclosure seriously. It is a reason I rely on the breadth and validation arguments and not on his own enthusiasm, and I am a macroeconomist with no IO stake. His concession that BLP results are sensitive to instruments and implementation is the caveat I carry into the vote.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B005 first after moving from B025. She argues that measurement tools can count as discoveries when they change what can be known, and that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum make B025's credit problem harder than B005's boundary question.
responses.response: Her analogy to measurement advances matches how I now see B005. Her move away from B025 because of the uncredited parallel contribution is also reasonable, and it is why I would not substitute B025 for B005 despite my own ranking of it fourth. Her round-1 claim that B027 is too close to 2022 is one I partly answered earlier. I still think the mechanisms differ, but I concede the overlap would be argued with the Committee and the evidence for the distinction is indirect.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B005 first. He says the citation should be honest that this is a methods prize and rest the merit case on the downstream record, and he now agrees that a two-person Kiyotaki-Moore award is better defined than adding Gertler.
responses.response: His point about honest wording is one I adopt in the citation, which names the methods and what they made measurable. His withdrawal of the Gertler proposal answers the chair's question about B027 from my side: I would not add Gertler or Gilchrist, so I treat it as confirmed from his round-1 text. It does not change my ranking now. B027 on its best form is a two-person prize with a clean attribution and an indirect validation record. B005 has the same attribution cleanness and a stronger record, which is why I place B027 second.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a broader empirical-IO citation that would bring in Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard or Levin. I would then want the citation and credit set changed together, and I have not weighed that configuration separately.

Whether a methods and measurement contribution should rank below a substantive or conceptual contribution. I read the common test as favouring B005, but that is a judgement about weights on which members differ, and the chair summary shows the disagreement is open.
How far BLP-type sensitivity to implementation, instruments and equilibrium assumptions should lower confidence in the empirical knowledge the method produced, as distinct from its originality.

Whether the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is distinct enough from the 2022 prize, and whether indirect validation should count against a contribution of this age. These facts affect my first alternative and I cannot settle them from the evidence supplied.
I have not independently verified any claims about prior prizes, citation counts, replication records or contribution dates. My statements rest on the opening, round-1 and chair-summary files.
statement.conflict_note: I disclose that I am the committee secretary, and that I am a long-term co-author of Timo Boppart (co-opted member, including the 2018 Myrdal Prize article) and John Hassler (chair), both colleagues whose arguments I address here. Boppart prefers B027 and Hassler prefers B014, so agreement or disagreement with them should not be read as independent confirmation. My field is macroeconomic theory, and B027 is the field closest to mine, which is one reason I discount my own round-1 preference. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn or to the credited names on B027 and B014. I record these ties as disclosures and do not adjudicate them.
